title: Backwards alphabetical
description: cities.txt holds one city per line, in no particular order. Print all of them in reverse alphabetical order, one per line, and nothing else. Example: the lines bern, oslo, lima -> oslo, lima, bern. Leave the file itself unchanged.
objective: Practise ordering lines in descending order.
check:
expected=$(printf 'zurich\noslo\nmadrid\nlima\nbern')
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected every city in reverse alphabetical order:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Numbers by value
description: sizes.txt holds one number per line. Print them from smallest to largest by numeric value, one per line, and nothing else. Example: the lines 10, 2, 30 -> 2, 10, 30. By default lines are compared character by character, which would put 10 before 2, so comparing by value has to be asked for explicitly.
objective: Practise ordering lines by numeric value instead of character by character.
check:
expected=$(printf '2\n9\n10\n30\n100')
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected the numbers from smallest to largest by value:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Highest score first
description: scores.txt holds one score per line. Print them from highest to lowest by numeric value, one per line, and nothing else. Example: the lines 10, 2, 30 -> 30, 10, 2. Both the numeric comparison and the descending order have to be asked for explicitly.
objective: Practise combining numeric comparison with descending order.
check:
expected=$(printf '120\n88\n45\n9\n7')
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected the scores from highest to lowest by value:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Sorted, no repeats, one command
description: tags.txt holds one tag per line, some of them repeated. Print each distinct tag once, in alphabetical order, one per line, and nothing else. Example: the lines go, c, go -> c, go. Do it with a single command and no pipe: the same command that puts the lines in order can also drop the repeats.
objective: Practise ordering lines and removing duplicates in one step.
check:
expected=$(printf 'c\ngo\nrust\nzig')
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected each distinct tag once, in alphabetical order:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi
if grep -q '|' "$CMM_COMMAND"; then
  echo "The output is right, but this card asks for a single command with no pipe."
  exit 1
fi

title: Sort a file into itself
description: names.txt holds one name per line, in no particular order. Change the file so its lines are in alphabetical order, keeping every line. Example: a file with the lines dan, amy, cid ends up holding amy, cid, dan. What gets printed does not matter, only what ends up in names.txt. Careful: redirecting a command's output straight back into the file it reads empties the file before it is read.
objective: Practise saving sorted output over the input file without losing its contents.
check:
expected=$(printf 'alice\nbob\ncarol\nmallory\nzoe')
if [ "$(cat names.txt 2>/dev/null)" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected names.txt to hold every name in alphabetical order:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "It holds:"
  cat names.txt 2>/dev/null || echo "(the file is gone)"
  exit 1
fi

title: Sort by one column only
description: staff.txt has three columns separated by single spaces: name, department, city. Print every line ordered by department alone. Lines in the same department must then appear in alphabetical order of the whole line, which here means by name. Example: the lines amy sales zurich, cid ops rome, bob sales oslo -> cid ops rome, amy sales zurich, bob sales oslo. Print nothing else. Naming only the column where the comparison starts is not enough: it would run on to the end of the line and let the city decide ties, so the comparison has to be told where to stop too.
objective: Practise limiting the sort comparison to a single column.
setup:
printf 'amy sales zurich
cid ops rome
bob sales oslo
dan ops lima
' > staff.txt
check:
expected=$(printf 'cid ops rome\ndan ops lima\namy sales zurich\nbob sales oslo')
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected the lines ordered by department, with names in order inside each department:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Colon records by number
description: ages.txt holds one record per line in the form name:age. Print every record ordered by age from youngest to oldest, comparing ages as numbers, and nothing else. Example: the lines alice:30, bob:8, carol:20 -> bob:8, carol:20, alice:30. Columns are split on blanks by default, so the colon separator has to be asked for explicitly, and so does comparing that one column by value.
objective: Practise sorting delimited records numerically by one field.
check:
expected=$(printf 'bob:8\ncarol:20\nalice:30\ndan:100')
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected the records from youngest to oldest by numeric age:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi
